entities.summary:
The Church of Notre-Dame of Dijon (Église Notre-Dame de Dijon), built primarily between 1220 and 1240 CE, is one of the finest examples of early Gothic architecture in Burgundy, France — remarkable for its highly unusual west façade featuring three arcaded galleries of blind arches decorated with 54 gargoyles (replaced in modern times after they fell), and for housing the celebrated 11th-century Black Madonna of Dijon (Notre-Dame de Bon-Espoir, 'Our Lady of Good Hope'), one of the most venerated Marian images in Burgundy and the center of major historical events.

Notre-Dame's architecture is genuinely exceptional: the west façade's three-story arcaded galleries (each level with two rows of pointed arches) create one of the most unusual compositions in French Gothic architecture, unlike any other major church of its period. The original 54 gargoyles (reproduced today after structural failures) were carved in the distinctive aggressive style of the Gothic grotesque tradition. The false tribunes of the façade have no counterpart in the Gothic canon, making Notre-Dame de Dijon a unique architectural document.

The 11th-century Black Madonna (carved ebony or dark-stained wooden figure) was carried in procession in 1513 and is credited with preserving Dijon from Swiss siege — creating the 'Jacquemart' bell tradition commemorating the victory. The same Black Madonna was processed again in 1944 when the city was liberated from German occupation, creating a tradition of the city's major crises being addressed through Marian procession. The church also houses the famous Jacquemart clock (a mechanical figure striking the hours), originally looted from Flanders by Philip the Bold of Burgundy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of Notre-Dame Dijon — with its uniquely experimental Gothic façade, the Black Madonna that twice saved the city, and the Jacquemart clock from Burgundian conquest — is one of France's most architecturally distinctive Gothic churches and a central monument of Dijon's civic and religious identity.
